title: I’m an NYC dad — here’s what Nikole Hannah-Jones got so wrong about our public schools ong-about-our-schools/
author: Sam Munson
summary: Novelist and New York City public school parent Sam Munson argues that Nikole Hannah-Jones wrongly ties school quality to racial and income demographics. His own children attend Title I, majority-Latino bilingual schools where committed teachers and principals have delivered a good to excellent education. He does credit one part of her critique: wealthy liberals will pay almost any price to avoid schooling their children alongside lower-income Black and Latino students, a bias he has witnessed among neighbors. Munson rejects racism and underfunding as explanations, pointing to Mississippi's NAEP gains for Black students, New York's charter results, and P.S. 307's $52,000 per-student funding. He calls for more screened schools, harder academic standards with real consequences, schools where non-gifted students flourish, and breaking the power of the unions and the education bureaucracy.
points: Munson's children thrive in Title I, majority-Latino schools, which he offers as evidence that demographics do not drive failure.
Progressive parents in his neighborhood have made obliquely racist remarks about his children's bilingual school.
Mississippi has raised Black fourth graders' NAEP reading and math scores to third among peers nationally.
He proposes expanding screened schools, hardening standards, and weakening union and bureaucratic protections.
He highlights Hannah-Jones's own line that students respond to the expectations of the adults who run their schools.
quotes: As a New York City public-school parent myself, what strikes me about Hannah-Jones’ narrative is how deeply she seems to connect racial and income demographics with school quality.
My own kids are growing up in Title I, majority-Latino schools where their education has been good to excellent.

The wealthy liberals who spent a decade beating their breasts about their own alleged complicity in “white supremacy” will bear any burden and pay any price to avoid educating their children in the same schools as lower-income black and Latino kids — no matter how high-quality those schools may be.

Combine such racial and class biases with an utter lack of accountability for failing schools and ever-eroding academic standards, and you’ve got the recipe for a perverse system in which the chief exponents of inclusion become exclusionists par excellence.
It must break the back of the unions and the DOE bureaucracy — chief patrons of teachers who don’t teach and administrators who don’t administer.
But look at Najya’s tragedy, which occurred even though she had a well-off, well-connected, powerful mother to advocate for her.
